w: Clovis was baptised here by Saint Remigius around 500 AD, and the Gothic cathedral that replaced an earlier fire-gutted church became the coronation site of French kings for centuries. Badly shelled in the First World War, it was restored and now draws about a million visitors a year as a UNESCO site.
s: Where French kings were crowned, since Clovis
_facts: Traditional baptism site of Clovis by Saint Remigius, c. early 6th century
Traditional coronation church of the kings of France; present cathedral built 13th-14th century replacing a fire-destroyed original
Severely damaged in WWI, restored in the 20th century; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991, ~1 million visitors a year

w: Sold off to Starwood Capital in 2005 along with a Loire Valley winery and the Hotel de Crillon in Paris, the Taittinger family clawed their own champagne house back a year later with backing from Credit Agricole. It's now run by Vitalie Taittinger, daughter of the man who sold the whole thing.
s: Champagne dynasty that bought back its own name
_facts: French champagne family, holdings once included Societe du Louvre, Concorde Hotels (Hotel de Crillon) and Bouvet-Ladubay
Sold to Starwood Capital in 2005; family reacquired Champagne Taittinger in 2006 with Credit Agricole backing
Currently headed by Vitalie Taittinger, daughter of Pierre-Emmanuel Taittinger

w: Built after 1870 as part of the ring of forts defending Reims, La Pompelle had already been stripped of its guns by 1913 - then took the heaviest bombardment dealt to any fort around the city once the First World War arrived. What survives still stands in ruin on the road toward Chalons-en-Champagne.
s: Ruined WWI fort that took the war's worst shelling
_facts: Fort built after 1870 as part of the Sere de Rivieres fortification system defending Reims
Disarmed 1913, saw the heaviest fighting of the Reims forts in WWI
Remains in a state of ruin near Sillery, between Reims and Chalons-en-Champagne

w: Founded in 1985 to house the private collection of Philippe Charbonneaux, this motor museum in Reims runs on one enthusiast's garage rather than any industry archive - a personal history of the automobile, parked in the middle of Champagne country.
s: One collector's cars, on show since 1985
_facts: Founded 1985 to house the car collection of Philippe Charbonneaux

w: Founded in Avize in 1811, this champagne house passed to Charles Nicolas de Cazanove, a botanist son who became a leading voice in the fight against phylloxera, the root louse that nearly wiped out Europe's vineyards. The family firm still turns out roughly 3 million bottles a year.
s: Champagne house built by a phylloxera-fighting botanist
_facts: Champagne producer founded in Avize in 1811 by Charles Gabriel de Cazanove
Developed by his botanist son Charles Nicolas de Cazanove, a leader in fighting phylloxera
Produces approximately 3,000,000 bottles annually

n: Monument to the Heroes of the Black Army
w: This is the Reims copy of a war memorial in Bamako, Mali, honouring the African soldiers of France's 'Armee noire' who helped defend the city in the summer of 1918. The Bamako original was inaugurated in January 1924; the Reims replica, standing today in the Parc de Champagne, followed that same July.
s: Reims' tribute to the African troops who held the line
_facts: Replica of a Bamako, Mali war memorial commemorating African soldiers who defended Reims in summer 1918
Bamako original inaugurated January 1924; Reims replica inaugurated July 1924
Located in Parc de Champagne, Reims

w: Known locally just as the PO, this luxury maison close opened in 1926 on the corner of the rue de la Magdeleine and rue Bacquenoi, its prestige said to rival Paris's most storied houses like the One-Two-Two. It closed for good in 1946, once France's Loi Marthe Richard shut every brothel in the country down.
s: The 'PO' - Reims' answer to Paris's grandest brothels
_facts: Luxury maison close (brothel) in Reims, opened 1926, on the corner of rue de la Magdeleine and rue Bacquenoi
Prestige said to rival Paris's One-Two-Two and Le Chabanais
Closed 1946 following the Loi Marthe Richard, which abolished brothels in France

w: One of only three 'front-line' cities Andrew Carnegie funded a library for after the First World War, alongside Leuven and Belgrade, Reims got this Art Deco building in the 1920s. It served as the city's main library until 2003 and is now protected as a monument historique for the elegance of its proportions alone.
s: Andrew Carnegie's Art Deco gift to a shelled city
_facts: Library built with Andrew Carnegie's donation after WWI; one of three 'front-line' cities given a Carnegie library (with Leuven and Belgrade)
Built in the 1920s, Art Deco decor; main library of Reims until 2003
Listed in the French inventory of monuments historiques

w: Founded in 1851 by Charles Camille Heidsieck, who earned the nickname 'Champagne Charlie' across Europe, this is the smallest of the Grandes Marques champagne houses - and one of the best regarded for both vintage and non-vintage cuvees. It has been part of the EPI group since 2011.
s: The smallest Grande Marque, founded by 'Champagne Charlie'
_facts: Smallest of the Grandes Marques champagne houses, based in the Reims region
Founded 1851 by Charles Camille Heidsieck, nicknamed 'Champagne Charlie'
Part of EPI group since 2011

w: Founded in 1730, this champagne producer predates the very idea of 'champagne' as a marketing category. These days it's better known for the wines it bottles under the Tsarine and Tsarina labels than for its own quieter name on the cellar door in Reims.
s: A 1730 champagne house behind the Tsarine label
_facts: Champagne producer founded 1730, based in the Reims region
Produces vintage and non-vintage cuvee, plus an extra dry series known as Tsarine and Tsarina
